title: The economist behind the ‘China shock’ says AI is a paradoxical ‘skill-disequalizer’ for Gen Z workers
key_facts: MIT economist David Autor and six co-authors published an NBER working paper, not peer reviewed, on a three-month experiment with 133 lawyers at 11 US intellectual-property firms.
Two-thirds of the lawyers were randomly given a then-unreleased Google Labs AI patent-drafting assistant.
The paper lists Autor's six co-authors as Google employees and says Google conducted the study and paid its direct costs.
After 90 days AI access raised drafting scores by 0.38 standard deviations, from less weak work rather than more excellent work.
In a final task without AI, senior lawyers (seven or more years) with AI access beat controls by 0.45 standard deviations; junior lawyers showed no average gain.
Autor calls AI a 'performance equalizer' but a 'skill-disequalizer' and warns young professionals of the 'illusion of competence'.

Caveats: only 91 of 133 lawyers finished the unaided test, no skills test at the start, 15 markups flagged as possibly AI-assisted, small sample from one client's firms, three months is short; the study did not examine Gen Z as a group.
Autor says firms that automate away formative practice 'sever the apprenticeship pipeline'.
quote_evidence: “Our results challenge the idea of AI being an automatic skill equalizer,” Autor said in written responses to Fortune. “Our data suggest that it’s a performance equalizer, but a skill-disequalizer, in that only practitioners who already had foundational mental models were able to level up their underlying skill sets.”
Senior lawyers who had AI access beat their control-group peers by 0.45 standard deviations, according to the paper. Junior lawyers showed no average gain.
Only 91 of the 133 lawyers finished the AI-free test.
why_it_matters_hint: Early-career workers may not build skills while AI does the drafting, in one small, Google-run study of patent lawyers.
event_date: Not stated for the paper; Fortune published 10 Oct 2026
notes: Whole Fortune article read. Working paper not peer reviewed; Google paid for and ran the study (Google says it is independent research Autor did as a fellow). Gen Z was not studied as a group.
